title: GOD SAW WHAT YOU DID WHEN THEY WERE TOO DRUNK TO PROTECT THEMSELVES.
paragraphs: GOD SAW WHAT YOU DID WHEN THEY WERE TOO DRUNK TO PROTECT THEMSELVES.
There is a sin that society disguises as entertainment, friendship, and harmless fun—but Scripture describes it with a terrifying word: WOE.
They trusted you.
That is what makes it so disturbing.

They thought they were surrounded by friends. They thought they were safe. They thought the laughter was innocent, the drinks were harmless, and the people encouraging them to have another round genuinely cared about them.
“Come on, just one more.”
“Don't be boring.”
“Relax. You're with us.”
And then something changed.

Their judgment became clouded. Their defenses weakened. Their ability to protect themselves diminished. What they would never willingly reveal while sober suddenly became accessible to people who had no right to exploit their vulnerability.
Someone started recording.
Someone started laughing.
Someone crossed a boundary.
Someone saw an opportunity where they should have seen a responsibility.
And somewhere between the laughter and the humiliation, a human being created in the image of God became somebody else's entertainment.
But heaven was not laughing.
Long before smartphones, viral videos, nightclubs, social media scandals, and drunken parties existed, God had already spoken against this kind of wickedness.
“Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness!” — Habakkuk 2:15 (KJV)
Read that again.
God did not merely condemn drunkenness in this passage. He condemned the deliberate exploitation of another person's intoxication for the purpose of exposing their nakedness.
The original Hebrew makes the moral seriousness unmistakable.
הוֹי מַשְׁקֵה רֵעֵהוּ מְסַפֵּחַ חֲמָתְךָ וְאַף שַׁכֵּר לְמַעַן הַבִּיט עַל־מְעוֹרֵיהֶם
The passage begins with the Hebrew word הוֹי (hôy), meaning “woe”—a prophetic expression of lament, denunciation, and impending judgment.
It is not a casual warning.
It is not God expressing mild disappointment.
It is a solemn declaration against wickedness.
The expression שַׁכֵּר (shakkēr) refers to making someone drunk, while לְמַעַן (lema‘an) introduces purpose, meaning “in order that” or “so that.”
That distinction matters.
The intoxication described here is connected to an intention. Someone deliberately weakens another person's condition in order to gaze upon their exposed nakedness.
The Hebrew expression מְעוֹרֵיהֶם (me‘orêhem) refers to their nakedness or exposed condition.

In its original historical context, Habakkuk 2 contains prophetic woes against the arrogant, violent, and oppressive Babylonian power. The imagery of drunkenness and nakedness communicates domination, degradation, and public humiliation.
We must not strip the verse from that context.
Yet neither should we ignore the moral evil that the imagery exposes.
God condemns the powerful who exploit the vulnerable, the arrogant who humiliate others, and those who turn another person's weakness into an opportunity for selfish gratification.
And suddenly, an ancient prophetic passage feels painfully contemporary.
Because Babylon's arrogance did not disappear with Babylon.
Its patterns still appear wherever human beings abuse power, manipulate trust, and celebrate another person's humiliation.
It appears when someone deliberately encourages another person to drink beyond their limits because they have an ulterior motive.
It appears when a man hopes alcohol will make a woman easier to manipulate.
It appears when a woman exploits an intoxicated man.
It appears when friends record someone in a humiliating condition instead of protecting them.
It appears when private photographs, intimate videos, embarrassing confessions, and vulnerable moments are circulated for entertainment, revenge, attention, or profit.
It appears when someone says, “They were drunk anyway,” as though another person's impaired judgment somehow removes their God-given dignity.
No.
Another person's vulnerability is not your permission. It is your responsibility.
Someone's intoxication does not give you ownership over their body, their privacy, their dignity, or their future.
A person who is incapacitated cannot give meaningful consent.
And someone else's sinful or unwise decision never grants you permission to commit another sin against them.
Scripture does warn against drunkenness.
Ephesians 5:18 says:
“And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.”
But the Bible's warning against drunkenness must never become an excuse to blame someone for the abuse another person chose to commit against them.
Both personal responsibility and the responsibility of the person who exploits another can be addressed without confusing the two.
God sees the difference.
Perhaps you are reading this with a memory you have spent years trying to bury.
A party.
A bedroom.
A photograph.
A message.
A video you never agreed to have shared.
A morning when you woke up terrified because you could not remember everything that happened the night before.
Perhaps people laughed at something that quietly destroyed you.
Perhaps the people who should have protected you became the very people you needed protection from.
And perhaps the most painful part was not simply what happened.
It was how everyone treated you afterward.
They whispered.
They joked.
They questioned your character.
They reduced your entire identity to one moment of vulnerability.
You became a story people told without ever asking how much it hurt you to live through it.
But listen carefully.
The shame someone inflicted upon you is not the measure of your worth before God.
You are not somebody else's entertainment.
You are not a leaked photograph.
You are not a humiliating video.
You are not the worst thing that happened to you.
You are a human being created in the image of God, and the evil someone committed against you does not erase that truth.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
Jesus does not look at wounded people the way a cruel crowd looks at a scandal.
He sees the person behind the story.
The tears behind the silence.
The fear behind the smile.
The wounds behind the reputation.
And the heart that desperately needs restoration.
But perhaps you are on the other side of this article.
Perhaps you were the one holding the camera.
Perhaps you encouraged someone to drink because you wanted something from them.
Perhaps you forwarded the video.
Perhaps you laughed.
Perhaps you crossed a boundary and later convinced yourself that it was not serious because everyone had been drinking.
Perhaps you have never confessed what you did.
And now, for the first time in years, something inside you is becoming uncomfortable.
Do not silence that conviction.
Do not hide behind the excuse that everyone else was doing it.
Do not confuse the absence of immediate consequences with the absence of divine accountability.
Because Habakkuk does not end the warning at verse 15.
The very next verse declares:

“Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD'S right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory.” — Habakkuk 2:16 (KJV)
The humiliation Babylon inflicted upon others would return upon it under God's judgment.
The oppressor who gloried in another person's shame would encounter shame himself.
The one who forced others to drink would face the cup of divine judgment.
The message is sobering.
God is not indifferent to what people do behind closed doors.
He is not fooled by popularity, reputation, religious appearances, or carefully constructed excuses.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that all things are exposed before the eyes of the One to whom we must give account.
You may have deleted the recording.
You may have erased the messages.
You may have convinced everyone that nothing happened.
But deleting evidence is not the same as repentance.
And escaping human consequences is not the same as receiving God's forgiveness.
Yet this is precisely where the Gospel becomes astonishing.
Because the God who sees everything is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to expose sin and leave sinners hopeless.
He came to save.
He came to redeem.
He came to transform people who could never cleanse themselves through excuses, religious performances, or carefully managed reputations.
Consider what happened at the cross.
Jesus was stripped of His garments.
He was mocked.
He was publicly humiliated.
People watched His suffering.
They divided His clothing among themselves, as recorded in Matthew 27:35.
The sinless Son of God endured the cruelty and shame of crucifixion.
Hebrews 12:2 tells us that He endured the cross, despising its shame.
The One who never sinned bore the judgment of sinners.
The One who possessed perfect dignity endured public disgrace.
The One who had every right to condemn us offered Himself as the sacrifice through whom repentant sinners could receive forgiveness.
At Calvary, human cruelty was exposed—and divine grace was revealed.
Jesus understands suffering and humiliation.
And through His death and resurrection, He offers something deeper than reputation management.
Redemption.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to continue harming people.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated as repentance, describes a change of mind that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning away from sin and turning toward God.
Real repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because you were caught.
It is not apologizing because your reputation is threatened.
It is not quoting Scripture to pressure the person you harmed into forgiving you.
It is acknowledging the evil of what you did, abandoning it, accepting accountability, and seeking to make appropriate amends without causing further harm.
It means respecting the boundaries of those you have wounded.
It means refusing to demand reconciliation.
It means cooperating with lawful accountability when necessary.
It means becoming someone who protects the vulnerable rather than exploiting them.
The forgiveness of Christ does not erase every earthly consequence of sin, but it offers repentant sinners reconciliation with God and the beginning of genuine transformation.
That is the difference between cheap excuses and costly grace.

And to those who have been wounded, please remember that forgiveness does not require you to return to an unsafe relationship, remain silent about abuse, abandon justice, or pretend that nothing happened.
Seeking protection, professional support, and appropriate legal accountability is not a betrayal of your faith.
You can pursue healing without giving someone another opportunity to harm you.
You can entrust judgment to God while establishing necessary boundaries.
You can belong to Jesus while still working through painful memories.
Healing is not always instantaneous.
Sometimes it comes through prayer, wise counsel, safe relationships, professional care, and many difficult days of learning to live without carrying the shame that others placed upon you.
But your story does not have to end where somebody else's cruelty began.

This is why the Church must become a place where vulnerable people are protected rather than exploited, where wrongdoing is confronted rather than concealed, and where grace is proclaimed without sacrificing truth or justice.
Romans 12:10 calls believers to honor one another.
Galatians 6:2 commands us to bear one another's burdens.
Philippians 2:4 teaches us to consider the interests of others.
Imagine how different our communities would become if Christians actually lived these truths.
Imagine being the friend who puts the camera down.
The person who refuses to forward the video.
The one who intervenes when somebody is being pressured.
The one who arranges safe transportation and appropriate help.
The one who refuses to participate in humiliating gossip.
The one who says, “That person needs protection, not an audience.”
That is what loving your neighbor can look like.
Not merely posting Bible verses.
Not merely wearing a cross.
Not merely calling yourself a Christian.
But allowing the character of Jesus to govern what you do when another human being is powerless to defend themselves.
Have you ever entertained yourself with another person's shame?
Have you shared something that should have remained private?
Have you mistaken someone's vulnerability for permission?
Have you remained silent when you knew somebody was being mistreated?
Or have you been carrying a wound that you desperately need to bring before Jesus?

You do not owe the internet the details of your trauma. You do not have to publicly confess private experiences to prove your faith. But your words of hope may remind another wounded soul that they are not walking alone.
Not because another post needs attention, but because someone among your friends may be silently carrying the consequences of the very evil Scripture condemns.
Someone may need the courage to seek help.
Someone may need to confront their own sin.
Someone may need to understand that Jesus offers a future beyond the scandal that has defined their past.
Your decision to share could help this message reach someone we might never otherwise reach.
The Gospel is freely given, but the work of producing, publishing, distributing, and expanding biblical resources requires practical support.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Giving is an opportunity to glorify God through generosity—not a transaction that purchases His favor, forgiveness, or salvation.
If God has placed generosity upon your heart and you are able to give, we warmly invite you to partner with us.
Because this mission has never been about purchasing grace.
It is about proclaiming it.
The world has enough people willing to expose someone's nakedness, circulate their shame, and profit from their humiliation.
What it desperately needs are people who will confront evil, protect the vulnerable, proclaim repentance, pursue justice, and introduce broken hearts to the redeeming love of Jesus Christ.
Be that person.
Be the friend who protects.
Be the believer who refuses to laugh.
Be the sinner who genuinely repents.
Be the disciple who chooses mercy without compromising truth.
And never forget that the same Jesus who calls the guilty out of darkness also welcomes the wounded into His care.
The world may remember the moment your dignity was stolen, but Jesus sees the life that is still worth restoring.
